source.title: Generalization Error of Generalized Linear Models in High Dimensions
source.authors: M Motavali Emami; Mojtaba Sahraee-Ardakan; Parthe Pandit; Sundeep Rangan; Alyson K. Fletcher

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and simulates double-descent behavior in generalized linear models using an asymptotic ML-VAMP/state-evolution framework, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study varies the sample count in synthetic GLM experiments and reports test-error curves. It does not sweep model size or training epochs. The reported 200 epochs for the nonlinear-regression optimizer is a fixed training setting, not an epoch-wise error sweep. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason:
The study derives exact asymptotic test error for GLMs and runs synthetic simulations sweeping sample count at fixed p. In under-regularized linear regression, test MSE rises with more samples while n

p. That is a direct result on sample-wise double descent (V3), reached by asymptotic theory rather than the original deep-network experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The conclusion section claims an exact procedure for the asymptotic generalization error of GLMs. It covers overparameterization, correlated covariates and train-test mismatch, with strong agreement between theory and simulations. The double-descent explanation is claimed in the abstract and in Section 5 and Appendix G.3 (ridgeless linear regression), not in the conclusion section.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an asymptotic high-dimensional GLM analysis based on ML-VAMP/state evolution and synthetic linear, logistic, and nonlinear-regression experiments; it does not reproduce the original deep-network method or settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports changes associated with feature correlation and train-test distribution mismatch. In linear regression, correlated features lower error slightly in the over-parameterized regime; mismatch increases test error.

fits_no_version.finding: For linear regression with Bernoulli ε-mismatch between training and test distributions, generalization error increases linearly with ε.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Train-test distribution mismatch raises generalization error linearly with the mismatch fraction in high-dimensional linear regression.

record.problems: The experiments are synthetic GLM settings rather than deep networks. Numerical curve values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text; the supplied text includes figure captions and discussion but not readable plotted values. For logistic and nonlinear regression, the text does not describe the test-error curve shapes.

untested.parts: There is no model-size sweep and no deep networks.
There is no epoch-wise test-error curve; the 200 ADAM epochs are a fixed setting.
Capacity is not swept. The analytic ridgeless formula is a function of β=p/N, but experiments vary N at fixed p, and a second descent with growing capacity is not examined.
No effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
There is no sweep toward optimal regularization, no label-noise isolation and no multiple peaks. The study only notes the effect occurs in highly under-regularized settings.

missing.what: Analytic ridgeless limit of test error. It is σd²/(1−β) for β<1 and β/(β−1)σd²+(1−1/β)σtr²Var(W⁰) for β≥1, so it diverges at the interpolation point β=p/N=1. The authors say this explains double descent for ridgeless linear regression.

record.verdict_notes: The linear-regression double descent recovers known results of Hastie et al. 2019, as the authors acknowledge. It is still the study's own derivation and simulation. There are no numeric values in the text, and all experimental evidence is figure-only. For logistic and nonlinear regression, the text does not say whether a peak appears, and logistic regression is not run ridgeless.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep is reported; the linear experiment fixes p=1000 and varies the number of samples.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The sample-count sweep is reported for synthetic GLMs, most explicitly for under-regularized linear regression. The paper does not quantify a peak location.
The experiments vary sample count, not capacity growing past an interpolation point.
The paper relates generalization error to parameters including the sampling ratio, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
The reported experiments do not test multiple peaks or whether an optimally tuned regularizer eliminates the peak; they do not isolate label noise as the cause of the peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.measure: Normalized test MSE in dB versus sample count
rows.note: The text says test MSE increases with more samples in the over-parameterized regime (n/p<1) and decreases again in the under-parameterized regime (n/p>1). State-evolution predictions are also plotted and are said to match simulations.

relationships.condition: Under-regularized (λ=1e-4) linear/ridge regression, i.i.d. or correlated features with matched train/test, p=1000, SNR 10 dB
relationships.reason: Test MSE rises as n grows toward p, then falls for n>p (r1, r2). The analytic ridgeless limit in Corollary 3 diverges at β=1, according to the text.
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE rose as n approached p and fell for n > p; the analytic ridgeless limit diverged at β = 1.
